subsubtopic: DELAY IN SALE OF CANADIAN FORCES BASE FALCONBRIDGE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I call on the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Mclnnes) and the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. de Cotret) to break the bureaucratic log-jam concerning the sale of Canadian Forces Base Falcon-bridge. A submission to Treasury Board was made on July 18 concerning alternate uses for the Base. The submission has the full support of the Sudbury community, as well as Public Works Canada, the Department of National Defence and, I am told, the Prime Minister's Office. The only result achieved to date has been mounting frustration. Is this simply another indication of the Government's lack of commitment to regional development? 1 certainly hope not.
I ask the Minister of Public Works to meet on an urgent basis with the President of the Treasury Board to resolve this matter speedily which, I reiterate, has the complete backing of the Sudbury community, and which appears to be delayed solely by bureaucratic bungling.

subsubtopic: PRIMATE OF POLAND'S VISIT TO CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we are honoured today by the arrival in Canada of his Eminence Cardinal Jozef Glemp, Primate of Poland, who begins a 10-day pastoral visit to this country. The Cardinal's home country of Poland has a population of some 35 million, over 90 per cent of which is Catholic.
His visit will be of inspiration to our many Polish-Canadian Catholics and provides a sharp contrast to the obstacles faced by over 2 million Poles presently living in the Soviet Union. In the hearts of those Poles the Cardinal enjoys a special affection. As Canadians we enjoy the freedom to worship. Catholics living in the U.S.S.R. must face harassment and even imprisonment should they dare to practise their beliefs openly.
I call upon my colleagues to join with me in welcoming the Cardinal to our shores and to wish him success in his efforts to provide Polish Catholics with inspiration and encouragement in the face of great adversity.

subsubtopic: U.S.S.R.-PLIGHT OF DISSIDENTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the release of Soviet dissident Yuri Orlov as an aftermath of the Daniloff affair has been welcomed as a step toward helping thousands who wish to emigrate from the Soviet Union. At the same time we are reminded of the extreme difficulties facing many of the other dissidents and the extraordinary measures that have been required to be taken by families and friends in the Soviet Union and support groups around the world, including Canada, to help them.
Many of Orlov's friends are still imprisoned in that country because they are members of persecuted Soviet human rights groups such as the Helsinki Accords Watch Committees. There are Russian, Ukrainian, and Armenian Watch Committees.
To give real meaning to the Helsinki Accords, I and other Members of this House call on the Government of the Soviet Union to respect the human rights of Yuri Orlov's friends, including Anatoly Marchenko, Antoly Kryagin, Josip Begin, Andrei Sakharov and many others by allowing them to leave the Soviet Union now.

subsubtopic: GOVERNMENT POSITION-PHARMACEUTICALS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have every reason to believe that the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Andre) is about to bury the drug patents legislation in an omnibus Bill which will include copyrights.
This strategy can have only one purpose, namely make Canadians swallow the Government's propositions on drug patents by diluting them in the urgent and essential reform of copyrights.
Mr. Speaker, it is unconceivable that the Minister would even consider equating the health of Canadians with the copyrights on a cookbook or a chainsaw.
It was a Liberal Government which, in 1969, made the drug industry more competitive by lowering drug prices, with the result that Canadians now pay less to remain healthy.
I hope the Minister will steer clear of an omnibus Bill designed to make Canadians swallow this pill.
I also hope the Minister will display enough courage to revise his legislation and bring it into line with the Eastman Commission recommendations. I can assure him that Canadian men and women will be ever grateful.
Stay healthy, Mr. Minister!

subsubtopic: REASONS FOR FUND-RAISING CAMPAIGNS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before September 4, 1984, the Liberal Government forgot to hand out one patronage favour- one that should have gone to Mrs. Campagnolo.
As reported in today's Globe and Mail, she is calling upon Liberal fund raisers to collect $75,000, an amount that would practically wipe out 30 to 40 per cent of the total tax savings those Liberals would be enjoying by making political contributions. How arrogant, how indecent!
This summer, the Liberal Party came up with a novelty of dubious taste by offering their donors to refund contributions on request, in the event donors were dissatisfied by December, 1986.
The most revealing survey is that the Liberal Party cannot even raise funds anymore. Canadian taxpayers will not pay for Mrs. Campagnolo's mortgage.

subsubtopic: RIDLEY TERMINALS, B. C.-REQUEST FOR INVESTIGATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have turned over to the Auditor General and the Commercial Crime Squad of the RCMP details of the financial affairs of the Ridley Terminals at Prince Rupert and Federal Commerce and Navigation.
Today I call on the Government of Canada to assist in this matter by immediately referring all books and documents related to this matter to the Auditor General and the RCMP.
A deal struck by the Liberals and continued by the Conservatives stands to rip off the taxpayers of Canada and the project for close to $1 billion. The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr. Mazankowski) is aware of the scandal and should demonstrate the leadership for which he is known, by revealing all federal documentation and protecting the taxpayers and the Ridley operation from further abuse.

subsubtopic: STORM DAMAGE CAUSED BY GREAT LAKES HIGH WATER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, high winds combined with high water levels on the Great Lakes Monday caused thousands of dollars of damage to a hotel in my constituency of Sarnia-Lambton. Forty-six rooms were awash with up to five inches of water. Strong northwest winds were up again yesterday, compounding the problem.
I am aware that the causes of the Great Lakes high water levels have been a natural phenomenon and I commend the actions of the Government in looking for possible solutions. The International Joint Commission is once again studying the possibility of implementing Plan 25N which could, over time, reduce water levels in Lake Erie. This would in turn reduce high water levels in Lake Huron. I urge the Government to ensure that the IJC study on 25N be completed as soon as possible. It is absolutely essential that all possible avenues be
October 8, 1986

explored, but we must move quickly on those which have already been studied. Immediate action and continued cooperation between Canada and the United States and the Province of Ontario could assist in the prevention of future disasters.

subsubtopic: FISHERIES PRODUCTS INTERNATIONAL-POSSIBLE CONSEQUENCES OF SHARE OFFERING
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Government of Canada is preparing to offer a $140 million share offering of Fishery Products International through a Toronto investment house. This is a share offering on a company that has received over $270 million in a public infusion of cash over the last number of years.
The people of Newfoundland, the workers in the fish plants and, indeed, the fishermen in the Province of Newfoundland, want to know why the Government is selling off this company at only 50 cents on the dollar. They want assurances that were given to be kept, that the jobs in the fish plants affected by this company will remain open despite the share offering. The Government of Canada should come clean before any sale is completed.

subsubtopic: EL SALVADOR-INCARCERATION OF HUMAN RIGHTS LEADERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, last year Canada restored financial aid to El Salvador on the grounds that President Napoleon Duarte would protect human rights. This year Duarte has proved Canada wrong. Four months ago Duarte's Government seized eight human rights leaders, tortured them, publicly accused them of belonging to the rebels, and to this day holds them incommunicado without charges, without court appearance, without means of defence.
Duarte's Government has also broadcast accusations that the Roman Catholic and Protestant churches give money to the rebels, an accusation which endangers the lives of church leaders. Canadians and Americans seeking to visit El Salvador, which is aided by our Government, to witness the massacre and bombing of civilian peasants and the selective terror against human rights leaders, have been harassed, sometimes jailed or even denied visas.
It is high time that Canada stop giving money to Duarte's regime and condemn the police and military terror of the Government of El Salvador.

subsubtopic: SOUTH AFRICA-CANADIAN ABSTENTION FROM ICAO VOTE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on the one hand the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) tells the House again and again that he is extremely concerned about the issue of apartheid. subsubtopic: VANCOUVER PORT LOCK-OUT-EFFECT ON SASKATCHEWAN ECONOMY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the lock-out announced yesterday of the longshoremen by the B.C. Maritime Employers' Association in the Port of Vancouver will have many devastating effects on the four western provinces. I am particularly concerned about grain farmers and potash producers in Saskatchewan. For example, the Saskatchewan potash industry will suffer immensely. There are seven Saskatchewan companies which mine potash, with sales through Vancouver totalling about three million tonnes per year.
Saskatchewan is a bulk supplier of grain and potash to world markets and should not be involved in this container dispute. Steps must be taken to regain the use of these facilities in Vancouver and Prince Rupert. I certainly commend the Minister of Labour (Mr. Cadieux) for his planned action taken in Thunder Bay and I hope similar action will be used here.
Longshoremen must come to terms with this dilemma and reinstitute operations in order to minimize the damage to western farmers and potash miners. This act of manipulation, the strangling of our resources, must come to an end. Yesterday would be none too soon.

speakeroldname: Hon. Frank Oberle (Minister of State for Science and Technology):
speakerposition: Minister of State for Science and Technology
subsubtopic: RESUMPTION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Both my predecessor and I have set a grueling pace for ourselves to meet with Canadians in all parts of our country. There have been several meetings with federal-provincial Ministers with respect to science and technology since our election two years ago. Earlier this year I held a series of round-table meetings with industrial leaders, union leaders and scientists across Canada. Last June in Winnipeg my provincial counterpart and I invited hundreds of leaders from labour, industry, universities and concerned organizations to a National Forum on Science and Technology. We asked the Science Council of Canada to chair this forum. Our dialogue moved us forward to our objective of achieving a new national consensus on policies for science.
Those who attended now realize that they have been heard by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) and Government because they see their recommendations reflected in the Speech from the Throne. They will recognize their suggestions in our plans for the months ahead. The consensus they have formed is forcefully expressed; it is urgent that all Canadian sectors take co-ordinated action without delay, that the federal Government is called upon to exercise decisive leadership, to unite every sector of our society so that Canada's full potential can be released.
The provincial and federal Governments must work together to forge a co-ordinated national policy. Science and technology must move to the centre of Government decision-making.
The consensus which has emerged also identified four critical issues which must be immediately addressed. The first has to do with creating a culture in Canada which appreciates and instils pride and celebrates Canada's scientists and innovators; which promotes a strong awareness of the importance to Canada today, and in the decades ahead, of astute application of science and technology; which utilizes the talents of Canadian women in science careers so that Canadian schoolgirls will know they too can succeed in technological careers and that their country needs their help in a technological age.
There is consensus that co-operative actions are needed to develop and mobilize Canada's greatest natural resource, our peoples' intellectual abilities and especially our scientific and engineering talent. We must expand the capacity of our universities to respond to new demands for basic research, and the training of researchers for exploration of new disciplines and the development of new skills.
There is a national consensus that we must urgently develop and use new strategic or, as they are now being called, "enabling" technologies which underpin our industrial capabilities. Canada, like all industrial countries, is undergoing a major transition from the technogies which have served us so well this far, technology we have had in place following the Second World War, to a new array of technologies which will be the basis for the creation of future growth and wealth; such as microelectronics, advanced information processing, advanced industrial materials and biotechnology, to name just a few. These technologies are the basis, and perhaps the cause,
The Address-Mr. Oberle
of the technological revolution. Our abilities with respect to these technologies will determine our economic fate.
Lastly, there was consensus that Governments should use the full scope of their instruments to advance research and development. Our regulatory framework, our tax laws and the incentives within them, our patent laws and similar instruments need to be re-examined to see how they can be targeted to encourage innovation and all aspects of scientific and technological activity. Engaging in dialogue and consultation and reaching consensus is an important prerequisite to taking important action. But talking and listening alone is no substitute for such action.
We have not hesitated to move ahead swiftly and decisively in areas involving federal jurisdiction. I would like to review some of the things that we have done. A number of science agreements were signed with the provinces to enhance industrial competitiveness and to use technology to reduce regional disparities. We moved ahead on a new funding policy which will provide resources to the granting councils in a predictable and consistent manner. We are also providing additional funds through these granting councils to help us forge linkages between universities and the private sector through a matching arrangement which will deliver $1 billion of new funds for research and development over a five-year period.
I say this with confidence because early indications show that this move, coupled with the tax incentives that are associated with it, will unleash an enthusiastic response. I am confident that the goal will be met and, indeed, that it will be exceeded, and that we will bring together our full potential to train highly-qualified personnel while at the same focusing on research in those areas which pose the greatest challenge and the greatest opportunity for Canada's future.
In May of this year a new comprehensive space plan was announced. An extensive internal review is reaching completion on the entire federal science and technology framework so that all federal resources dedicated to science can be focused on new national priorities in a consistent manner. This is the first time that such an inventory has been put together. I anticipate that the Standing Committee on Research, Science and Technology, which was established during the last session of Parliament, will play an important part in evaluating the results of that review and of how the federal Government can spend much smarter and more effectively the $4.2 billion that we presently spend on science and technology and related activity.
Recently, we announced funding support to aid the innovative activities of the Canadian Institute for Advanced Research which networks together the best and brightest of our scientists and engineers across Canada in a new type of a fellowship program dedicated to excellence. A similar institute was formed in British Columbia with federal support.

October 8, 1986
The Address-Mr. Oberle
Building on the national consensus and on the initiatives which we took in the first session of this Parliament, we are now ready to take new actions on the agenda for the next two years, which was set out in the Speech from the Throne. The Speech from the Throne clearly indicates that the Government recognizes the threat that we will face and the bitter price that we will pay if we do nothing.
The Speech from the Throne announced the opening of a major effort to carve out a significant place for science and technology in the culture of Canada. In the past, lack of leadership and lack of prestige caused many Canadian students and the brightest of our scientists to turn to careers in other countries rather than to the careers of tomorrow in Canada. Science lacked the visibility and the prominence that would cause educators and the media to give it the attention it merits as a determining factor in our future. One of our principal priorities is to establish a new environment which gives value and appreciation to scientific achievement applied to improving our well-being and to resolving long-standing problems.
For the first time Canadians have a Prime Minister who is demonstrating this by meeting, on a regular basis and in a formal way, with Canada's most eminent scientists, engineers, and leaders from business, industry and labour. He will personally chair this new board or council. It will assess our national goals and policies regarding science and technology and their application to improve Canada's competitiveness and maintain prosperity. Its members will give the Prime Minister and Canada the benefit of their judgment, their wisdom and their experience.
We also announced that the Government will introduce a new federal science and technology strategy to support our policies and our mandate and to build on initiatives which are already under way. It is to be expected that new realities mean new strategies. Just as industry is having to restructure and adopt new attitudes to the reality of the new age, Government also has to re-examine and rationalize its activities and its policies which are leading the nation across a new frontier.
Many federal activities and programs have served this country well in bringing us this far along the way. However, resources are too scarce these days, too hard won, to be wasted. No part of the federal machine can expect to survive if it does not adjust to new priorities and do its share to meet new needs. All activities must be examined to determine if they can be performed with better results in universities, for instance in the area of basic and curiosity-type research, or contracted out to private scientific enterprises outside of Government.
One immediate example of Government reorganization in the face of new realities was announced in the Speech from the Throne. Legislation will be introduced to establish a Canadian space agency. Such an agency is needed in Canada if we are to be able to contribute the talent and ingenuity of its people to the peaceful use of space, to develop space technologies for applications to human problems.
The Prime Minister has asked me to reorganize our current efforts and to focus key space activities under a single agency which can operate with day-to-day autonomy while at the same time being held accountable to Government and to Parliament. I anticipate that personnel would be transferred from existing programs to staff the new centralized agency. The new agency will be accountable to the Government and to Parliament through the Minister of State for Science and Technology. The structure and the organization of the agency will reflect a broad, co-operative approach. The structure must be able to secure the active involvement of the private sector and our universities and institutes. Our policy will be to emphasize contracting out research and development so as to tap the expertise in all regions of Canada, especially the expertise that resides with small enterprise.
As well, I see a meaningful mechanism which will fully engage Canada's private sector capacity in advising the agency. I am beginning consultations with my colleagues immediately with a view to bringing this legislation-setting up the agency-before the House as soon as possible. The agency will have a double responsibility. It will, of course, first and foremost be responsible for the over-all quality of Canada's international contributions to space science and technology, including existing arrangements we presently have with Japan, the European community and, of course, the American space agency. It will also oversee Canada's domestic objectives related to space. These domestic responsibilities are very important because we see space development as one of the principal forces behind Canada's economic growth.
Robotics developed for use in space will have applications at the bottom of our mines and on the floor of our oceans. The applications of remote sensing and satellite communication technologies will help Canadians to bridge vast distances, making remote communities and remote resources more accessible. Space technologies will enable us to improve the custodianship of our natural resources, to enhance our environment, to strengthen our resource industries and the 350 cities and towns across Canada which depend upon them, places such as Prince George, Tumble Ridge and Mackenzie in my riding, Chicoutimi and other places throughout the country which depend on one or the other of our important resource industries for their life-blood.
This means the new agency will have a mandate to diffuse space technolgy into the private sector so that this knowledge can be put to work throughout Canadian industry. The money which we will spend on space must and will be used to keep Canada competitive.
The Speech from the Throne announced two major initiatives as part of our continuing efforts for broad national consultation and building consensus.
First, we are proposing a national forum on post-secondary education to strengthen our partnership with the provinces so that the Canadian system can produce the highly qualified
October 8, 1986

personnel which Canada needs to keep us on the crest of this competitive wave and to promote Canada's well-being. Second, building on the success of the National Forum in Winnipeg, we will hold another National Conference on technology and innovation broadening the access to this conference so that more Canadians can participate. I expect to consult soon with the various sectors on how best to organize this process.
We are totally dedicated to these tasks. The initiatives we have proposed will put science and technology to work to support our objectives, especially to build a national capacity to compete strongly in international markets and thereby keep Canadians employed. As was said in the Throne Speech, to a considerable degree our sense of national purpose, our national identity and our economic prosperity will depend on our capacity to respond, and respond we will. I believe all Parties are in agreement that we must take long-range action. That is why we have made our plans for a federal science and technology policy with an eye on the next generation and the next century, not with an eye on the next election.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first I should like to congratulate our new Speaker on his election to the position of Speaker of the House of Commons. Second, I should like to congratulate you, Sir, on your reappointment as Deputy Speaker and to congratulate the other Speakers who were reappointed or appointed for the first time. Also I should like to congratulate the mover and seconder of the Address in Reply to the Speech from the Throne. Although I did not agree with everything they said in their speeches, I still congratulate them for defending what some of us on this side of the House have already said was virtually indefensible.
In my remarks today I will address only one portion of the Speech from the Throne. I know that the Government would like to discuss its so-called four pillars. It now wants them to be known as the four pillars that care, or the four pillars with a caring face. However, the four pillars as set out in the Throne Speech are so vague that they obscure the Government's true record. One cannot see the policies for the pillars. One has to read between the lines or peer between the pillars themselves to get a true picture of how the country is being governed.
Let us concentrate on just one pillar-constructive internationalism. To be fair, there have been some successes in this regard. For example, the Government has sensed the revulsion which Canadians feel toward apartheid and used that consensus to promote the use of sanctions among western democracies. However, if we examine the Government's record in peace and security, the story is quite different. One page of the Throne Speech tells us:
No task is more important to Canadians than preserving peace and security.
That is the kind of simplistic statement which brought so much scorn on the Government's Grey Paper on Canada's foreign policy. Decima Research must have collaborated with the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) on that page at least.
However, if this desire for peace and security is so obvious, what has the Government done to meet the expectations of Canadians? The answer is, precious little. Just look at the ringing declarations which follow. The Government is "encouraged" that the superpowers are talking again. It "shares the hope" that there will be progress on arms control.
October 8, 1986

However, what has the Government done to promote disarmament? When the Soviet Foreign Minister was here, did the Government press the Soviets to move from a unilateral moratorium on nuclear testing to direct negotiations on a comprehensive test ban? Did the Government offer its seismic array in the Northwest Territories as part of a world-wide network to enforce such a treaty? Only yesterday the Secretary of State for External Affairs declined even to join in a unanimous resolution of the House in support of a comprehensive test ban.
When the White House announced that SALT II was dead, did the Government tell President Reagan that Canada would no longer test the Cruise missile which will breach SALT II's limits? When Canada had a chance to support the ABM Treaty by reinserting a clause in the NORAD agreement which precluded our taking part in ballistic missile defences, did the Government seize that opportunity? No, Mr. Speaker, the Government did not. The Government's pillar of peace and security crumbled when Mr. Reagan was involved.
Nowhere was this more obvious than in the Government's response to the American invitation to take part in star wars. The Government could not bring itself to say no to a dangerous escalation of the arms race. Instead, it wavered and supported private participation as long as the Government's hands looked clean in public.
Even when provoked by the Polar Sea incident, the Government failed to stand up for Canadian interests. The paragraph devoted to Arctic sovereignty is nothing but brave talk. The Government drew straight baselines around the Arctic Archipelago, but straight baselines are not a picket fence which will keep out American ice-breakers or Soviet submarines.
The truth is that the Government has done precious little in the Arctic to assert our sovereignty and acknowledges this fact in the Throne Speech. It is forced to talk about its past promises on sovereignty in the future tense. It must be galling for the Secretary of State for External Affairs to hear his unfulfilled promises hung out to dry in the Throne Speech.
Once again the Government proclaims that it will build an ice-breaker. This promise has been around long enough to demonstrate the Government's lack of resolve. Instead of uniting the country in asserting our sovereignty, it has divided us. The Cabinet is squabbling over who should pay for it. The starving shipbuilding industry is fighting over who should get the contract to build it. It is pitting East Coast shipbuilders against West Coast shipbuilders. I do not even know what the ice-breaker is supposed to do when it hits those icy waters; neither does the Department of National Defence. That is why it does not want to foot the bill to build the Polar 8 icebreaker.
Of course it is not really surprising that the Department of National Defence is dragging its heels. It does not like to hear about new expensive commitments from the Secretary of State for External Affairs. A case in point is the exercises announced
The Address-Mr. D. Blackburn
for the eastern Arctic in the Secretary's sovereignty statement. It turns out that the military did not know about any such exercises when the Secretary made his pledge. Eventually, a diving ship and a supply vessel were sent north to save face. Now the Government is once again pledging "training exercises in the Arctic".
By and large the Government's commitment to sovereignty is the same as its record on disarmament-all talk and no action. This is quite in contrast to the Department of National Defence where we have seen some real movement. The Hon. Member for Cumberland-Colchester (Mr. Coates) moved out and the Hon. Member for Yukon (Mr. Nielsen) moved in. Then he made room for the present Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Andre) who in turn passed the reins to the new Associate Minister of National Defence (Mr. Dick) when the present Minister of National Defence (Mr. Beatty) appeared.
All this movement has made for a curious situation. The Government has failed to keep its promise made in the previous Throne Speech to re-examine Canada's defence policy. I understand that no Minister wants to get into a policy discussion until he understands the subject matter, but the delays are becoming ridiculous and embarrassing.
In preparing this speech I discovered in my files a letter written to the first Minister of National Defence of this Government asking that he refer his Green Paper to the Standing Committee on External Affairs and National Defence early in 1985. We are rapidly approaching 1987, we no longer have the same Minister of National Defence, the Government no longer speaks of a Green Paper, and there is no longer a standing committee for both external affairs and national defence in combination.
While we have been waiting for the policy paper, the Department of National Defence has been busily entrenching our existing national defence commitments. I now doubt that the Government could afford to substantially alter any of the roles of the Armed Forces. This Conservative Government's actions have locked it into the philosophy of the Liberal Government's 1971 WhitePaper.
In the previous Throne Speech the Government recognized that the strategic context had changed considerably since the 1970s. I would go further than that. I would say that our present defence policies have their origin in the 1940s. The Government, in other words, is preparing us to fight World War II all over again in its strategic architecture.
Look at our commitments in Europe, for example. We have promised to send the CAST Brigade to reinforce Norway if that country faced invasion. The Government has just completed Exercise Brave Lion to practise this operation. Some 5,500 soldiers and 15,000 tonnes of equipment were shipped across the Atlantic. The Government has not put a price tag on this operation but the figure of $100 million has

October 8, 1986
The Address-Mr. D. Blackburn
been bandied about in the media. How could the Government ever reconsider the CAST commitment after spending $100 million, or even half that amount, on a dry run? Could it ever explain such an about-face to the Norwegians, especially after leaving some equipment behind until our forces return? The Government is effectively committed to Norway because it must justify the expense and portray Exercise Brave Lion as a great success.
Let us now look at Canada's other commitments to Europe. Could the Government re-evaluate our commitment in Germany, that is to the NATO central flank? I doubt it very much. It has already entrenched our positions there with its earlier measures. The Government sent an additional 1,200 men to Germany in the first months of being in office to show that Canada was, to use their words, pulling its weight. It would be very difficult to redeploy those men despite the fact that basing them in Europe is extremely expensive. In fact, our commitment to the European central flank, which every expert acknowledges is more political than military, is costing Canadians $100 million a year.
The Government is also spending millions of dollars to equip the forces for their present role in Europe. For example, the Government announced just last spring that it would buy a new low-level air defence system to protect our forces and their bases in Europe. The cost of this system alone is $1 billion. The Government does not even expect delivery until 1991. How could it seriously question the role of the Armed Forces in Europe, as many experts are now doing, having allocated $ 1 billion for equipment to be used there in the next decade? Neither could the Government consider changing its air commitment to the central front. It declared that role "sacred" by equipping our three squadrons in Germany with the CF-18 before the new fighters were fully deployed in Canada for national defence purposes.
The Government has committed us to Norway and Germany by its actions but our forces are unable to handle both roles. Our chief of defence staff was recently quoted as saying: "If we had to do everything simultaneously-no, I think we're stretched too thin. That must be acknowledged." The Government has not acknowledged that fact. Instead, it has been busy stretching our forces even further with a new peace-keeping role in the Sinai Peninsula. This is another open-ended commitment that costs $5.5 million per year.
We would all agree that peace-keeping is laudable and Canada receives world recognition for its contributions in this area. However, we are already firmly entrenched in Cyprus and on the Golan Heights and there are no signs of early settlement to any of these conflicts. The Government must recognize that peace-keeping ties up personnel and resources, and adjust its other commitments to allow for that.
At sea the Government is also committed to some very expensive long-term programs that will determine the character of our Navy and dictate its future role. No one would argue that our Navy is in desperate need of new equipment, but again the Government is acting before considering the future
role of Maritime Command. The TRIBAL Class Update and Modernization Program, sometimes referred to as TRUMP, will spend $1.2 billion to ensure that our destroyers will be able to provide air defence as traditional convoy escorts. The Government has also announced a program to replace the Sea-King helicopter. Some say this program will end up costing $2 billion by the time the new helicopters are flying. Again, Canada is committed to an anti-submarine warfare role well into the 1990s and beyond. Our own submarines need replacing. The Government announced a program to size up new candidates for another large puchase. No one has yet even ventured a guess on the eventual final price for those new submarines.
There have been other major expenditures but I think my point has been made. The Government has effectively precluded any meaningful debate on the future role of Canada's Armed Forces by taking actions which will dictate their posture for at least another decade. This, I think, is very, very important.
This Government came to power some two years ago first of all promising a Green Paper in which there would be national input from coast to coast, from experts, from academics, from ex-military professionals, and from ordinary Canadians. That has now gone by the board. I do not know on how many occasions this Government has promised a White Paper, a blueprint, a framework, an architecture for Canada's national defence, to plan and to pursue and effectively put into operation a policy designed not just for the 1980s but presumably for the 1990s. We are not going to get either, although the present Minister indicates there will probably be a White Paper some time this winter or early spring.
It is no wonder that the Throne Speech made no mention at all of a plan to review Canada's defence policy. I know the new Minister has committed himself to bringing a policy paper forward some time in 1987, but you will forgive me for saying that I have heard that before and I will believe it when I see it.
If the new Minister is really interested in a full and open debate, I have a suggestion for him. He might want to issue an early Green Paper for public discussion. In other words, go back to the original intention of the Government in 1984. That way he would not have to espouse the policies which are the legacy of his many predecessors, and I am not just talking about his predecessors in this Government but his predecessors in former Liberal Governments. Neither would he have to defend the intricacies of a comprehensive new policy. He can learn from the ensuing debate at the same time as he benefits from full public consultation. It would certainly be a refreshing change and it would fulfil the original commitment of the Government which was for a Green Paper, not a White Paper, as I mentioned a moment ago. In conclusion, that would show that the Government does indeed recognize how strongly Canadians feel about peace and security by giving Canadians the opportunity to tell the Government what kind of defence policy they want.
October 8, 1986

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in my maiden speech in the House of Commons as Minister of State for Youth, perhaps I may be allowed, first of all, to congratulate you on your appointment to the prestigious position of the Deputy Speaker of this House. I also would like to ask you to transmit a message that to me is very important, considering the importance of the Speaker's chair. It is a message of congratulations to the new Speaker (Mr. Fraser) of this House, wishing him the very best of luck.
Mr. Speaker, today, I would like to talk about the specific challenges, opportunities and problems the current situation presents for young Canadian men and women. These challenges go beyond those encountered on the labour market. Rapid technological change has necessarily had a major impact on education and of course on our society.
Mr. Speaker, this new era is the result of global changes that are occurring faster than ever before. The labour market, in fact our whole culture, is going through a period of transition comparable to the Industrial Revolution. We are part of an international community that is both more competitive and more interdependent than in the past. The oil crisis of the 70s made this abundantly clear.
Change is the order of the day. Markets rise and fall at an unprecedented rate, and the demand for various skills is constantly changing and shifting.
There is no quick and easy way to deal with this reality, whether we are speaking globally or internationally. However, as a nation and as a Government, we have no right to ignore these facts, and we must adopt the approaches and strategies that will help us to manage change where possible and to avoid being alienated by change.
To deny these new realities, Mr. Speaker, would be nothing less than disastrous, not only for Canadians but especially for our Canadian youth.
The Government must act as a catalyst, helping to define what the challenges are and where our collective responsibilities lie, and helping people understand what kind of opportunities the future holds in store. Some of the possibilities were referred to earlier by my colleague, the Minister of State for Science and Technology (Mr. Oberle); a new culture based on the continuing acquisition of knowledge, as my colleague mentioned, opens up almost unlimited opportunities for society in general and for the Canadian labour market in particular.

October 8, 1986
The Address-Mr. Charest
The impact of technology on the labour market is one of the main concerns of young Canadians. Our ability to integrate new skills and to create jobs commensurate with those skills is a reflection of our country's success to adjust to this rapidly changing environment, where competition is becoming increasingly fierce.
If young people do not get adequate training, if they are not provided with the means to adapt themselves, they will simply not be in a position to preserve Canada's prosperity and secure our economic future. The Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) recognizes it is urgent to integrate our young people properly into the labour force and, in that respect, Mr. Speaker, this Government's decision to link up the youth component to the Department responsible for employment matters is significant.
This new reality must also allow for participation by visible minorities, natives and the handicapped, who are an integral part of the gainfully employed population.
I am committed to doing everything humanly possible to promote the interests of those groups, feeling as I do that there can be no genuine economic, social and cultural progress without the full participation of all Canadian men and women.
New technologies in changing markets and the need for more advanced skills are the current challenges which our young people, who will be part of our labour force, should be able to take up. The training of that new, more flexible manpower endowed with more specialized knowledge, will require the co-operation of the young people themselves, the teachers, the labour unions, the private sector and all levels of Government.
The new technological era also entails other changes, new ways of defining work, a different view of hierarchy in the workplace, a new way of managing work and leisure hours. Actually what we are talking about is a new lifestyle, whence the need for autonomy and innovation.
In the light of those changes, we are reviewing certain programs. In consultation with the provinces, the labour unions and the business world, we will review such things as the apprenticeship training program, which to a large extent is funded by the Canada Employment and Immigration Commission. That review will take place over the next six months, with a view to determining the best possible avenues for getting labour and the training sector closer together.
We are also looking at measures to fight against illiteracy in Canada. In the same spirit, we are considering action to encourage young people to remain in school as long as possible, and measures to prevent drug abuse and help young offenders.
To promote access to employment, we are constantly improving our occupational counselling and employment information programs and we are developing new training tools for occupational counsellors. In this regard, we are
looking at the co-operation mechanisms between the Employment and Immigration Commission and the provincial Departments of Education. Similarly, the National Conference on Secondary Education announced by the Prime Minister for the beginning of 1987 and the proposed National Advisory Board for Industrial Technology will help to define the concepts, to develop the new mechanisms and to determine the levels of co-operation required for a better management of changes in these sectors.
Mr. Speaker, major progress was made in this direction a little over a year ago when the Canadian Jobs Strategy was implemented. This strategy represents a basic change in the federal policy as concerns training and job creation, especially for young people who, I should point out in passing, are the main users of these programs as a whole.
In summary, Mr. Speaker, 1 shall be looking, with the representatives of the provinces, the leaders in our society and young people, at ways to answer one basic question: What kind of direction do our young people need, not only to move successfully from the academic world into the active world, but also to become the nucleus of a labour force of international standing? The performance of Canada on the international scene is closely dependent on the answer to that question. In the short term, however, we must maintain our efforts in order to solve the unemployment problem among young Canadians, although the demographic process itself should progressively reduce the relative importance of this problem with which all industrialized nations are faced. In the present context, the ultimate irony is that we may face a manpower shortage in the years to come.
Statistics concerning unemployment among young people in all industrialized nations clearly indicate that everywhere governments must step up their effort with a view to integrate young people into the labour force during this transition period. In the United Kingdom, the unemployment rate among young people is nearly 22 per cent. In France, it exceeds 25 per cent, while in Italy and Spain, it exceeds 35 per cent and 43 per cent respectively.
In Canada, the unemployment situation among young people is not as serious as elsewhere, and it is improving. It went from nearly 19 per cent down to less than 15 per cent over the past 18 months. The cynicism and despair expressed by some of our youth are not as acute as elsewhere and, while travelling throughout this country, I have noted clear signs of increasing assurance and optimism among our young men and women who are aware that this country belongs to them and who are determined to develop it fully. The situation is not as critical as it is elsewhere, but as was indicated in the Throne Speech, much remains to be done. The distribution of jobs at the national level is very uneven: youth unemployment varies from around 10 per cent, its lowest level, in the Toronto area and goes on to exceed 30 per cent in Newfoundland. For native young people, the situation is even worse.
October 8, 1986

The Government has a duty to identify policies and clarify objectives in order to deal with these problems. Alone, however, it cannot provide easy answers. All sectors have a role to play in helping Canadians adjust to a changing job world, and in its role as national coordinator, the Government must ensure that the measures being taken by various sectors complement each other.
This Government's job strategy reflects the realization that solving the problem of youth unemployment does not depend on how many jobs are created but also on the type of jobs, real jobs that are career-oriented, for which real training is provided. The job strategy makes it possible to take into account both the technological changes taking place on the labour market and the priorities of each participant. The strategy emphasizes autonomy and innovation, two factors that are now indispensable to economic growth.
Mr. Speaker, the job strategy has no connection with any of the so-called band-aid solutions that may have been proposed before.
Taking its cue from this approach, the federal Challenge '86 program, aimed at creating summer jobs for young people, has set long-term objectives. With the support of local businesses and community organizations, Challenge '86 has helped create
90,000	jobs, which in most cases are related to the goals and aspirations of our young people.
The strategy's other programs, which run 12 months a year, are also based on these principles. The Job Entry Program features on-the-job training and practical work experience which are a solid basis for young Canadians to begin new careers. Then there is the Innovations Program to help those who have creative ideas and projects which propose fresh and innovating solutions to the labour market problems and create openings for technological applications.
As well, Mr. Speaker, the Speech from the Throne stresses the importance of finding new ways to instil the spirit of entrepreneurship in the minds of young people. We have already begun to work on this and will soon be in a position to unveil a major initiative in this field.
New trends are beginning to appear, such as team work and a growing awareness of the importance of quality and flexibility. Unless they can readily adapt to the changing situation and make the best of it, neither young people nor the various labour market interests can ever look forward to a productive future. Only a positive and flexible attitude coupled with longterm planning can foster prosperity among individuals and organizations.
Given the scope of the challenge facing us, it is only through a concerted national effort that we will succeed in fully integrating young people into the economic activities of this country and into society as a whole. For my part, besides defending the cause of young people in Cabinet and encouraging them to take full advantage of all services and programs offered by the federal Government, I will also strongly support
The Address-Mr. Charest
all measures likely to give youths more opportunities to become active participants.
The Advisory Counsil on Youth will make mechanism such as the Canadian Youth Foundation easier to be directly involved in the quest for solutions to their employment problems and other questions which concern us all.
The era of new technology offers young Canadians more opportunities for training, employment and personal development than any other previous period in history. All of us will have to use our minds and creativity to benefit socially and economically from these opportunities.
Mr. Speaker, we are living during an exalting period of transition, at a crucial time when we can experiment with new methods and discover new concepts, values and options to pave the way for a new society where all Canadians will be at home. If all of us, young people, educators, employer organization and union leaders, community leaders and elected representatives, are determined to get the most out of these opportunities, we shall prepare a great future for young Canadians and the nation, as a whole.
Finally, I am convinced that, like the previous generations, this one in 1986 will be able to overcome the obstacles it has inherited from others. Our basic message to young Canadians is that they must remember that Canada is still a country to be built and that they will build it for themselves and in their own image.

They say that the past is our guarantee for the future, but look at what happened to social justice under this Conservative Government and this Prime Minister, after what they said in the Speech from the Throne, look at the reality and at the reasons why we are now starting a new session.
About social justice and the elderly, Mr. Speaker, just a while ago, the Minister of State for Youth (Mr. Charest) scolded me for rising in the House to criticize the Government, Mr. Speaker. But I was proud to rise in support of the elderly, to save their Old Age Security pension cheques, while the Minister of State for Youth was busy protecting his own little portfolio.
Mr. Speaker, everyone will recall what the Prime Minister said during the election campaign. Everyone remembers what the Minister of social injustice and the Prime Minister said here in the House, and the Speech from the Throne and the blue Book on consultation and the nation-wide betrayal of our senior citizens. The first time senior citizens were betrayed and deceived by this Government was when family allowances were de-indexed. And the second time, Mr. Speaker, again in the Speech from the Throne, senior citizens were discriminated against, those between the ages of 60 and 64, with respect to the spouse's allowance. Once again, Mr. Speaker, all elderly Canadians-mostly women-in every single riding from sea to sea have heard this Government deliberately refuse to declare them eligible under the Old Age Security pension program simply because they had to separate, because they preferred to remain single, or because they were forced to seek a divorce. Mr. Speaker, this Government, including the Prime Minister and his social injustice Cabinet colleague, deliberately perpetuate such inequity, and now they are trying to make elderly Canadians believe that the 1986 Speech from the Throne is even better than the one we got in 1984. Mr. Speaker, we need look no further than what happened to the early retirees who expected to get their unemployment benefits in 1985 and 1986. Again thousands of Canadian men and women were penalized, they were deceived by this Government with regard to benefit cut-backs, with the result that some of them lost as much as $10,000. More phoney promises and more phoney commitments from this Government, Mr. Speaker. The 1984 Speech from the Throne was long on rhetoric, as is the 1986 Speech from the Throne. They said the same thing about the New Horizons Program, Mr. Speaker: When it comes to elderly Canadians, we will never do anything to harm them. Well, Mr. Speaker, behind their backs the Prime Minister and his Government did slash the benefits of elderly Canadians. During the first two years of this Government, not a single Conservative Member or Minister had the courage to rise in defence of our senior citizens.
Mr. Speaker, we should also recall the commitments made by the Prime Minister in the 1984 Speech from the Throne, particularly with respect to Canadian families, the cornerstone of our society, he said. The Prime Minister is never at a loss for words, they flow like money which is no problem when he wants to take his butler along on his world-wide trips. So what happened to Canadian families, Mr. Speaker? In 1984 the Prime Minister promised that the House would look after Canadian families, but he ended up de-indexing family allowances while at the same time introducing legislation to rescue Western Canada millionnaires from a bank failure. So much for the intellectual integrity of this Government and this Prime Minister, Mr. Speaker, and today in 1986 they would have us believe that people will swallow this piece of trash. Mr. Speaker, the child tax credit changes have victimized, middle-income families.
Mr. Speaker, senior citizens were deceived by this Government in 1984, and the Members opposite are now trying to make us believe .. . Look at what has been written. There are no concrete results. Families were deceived in 1984, Mr. Speaker.

Mr. Speaker, I want to commence by extending to the Speaker, his deputies and the new process my best wishes. I wish you and yours well.
I rise today to express a concern for rural Canada, not only for the food producers and other persons who live from the resources of the land but also for the towns, villages and hamlets which dot the country. The census of 1891 reported that 82 per cent of Canadians lived in rural areas. Today 4 per cent of Canadians live on farms and an additional 16 per cent live in rural non-farm situations.
I assert that the pattern of our population settlement is now reason for legitimate concern. Fifty-seven per cent of Canada's population is held within the 23 largest cities. Seventy-nine point five per cent of the Canadian population is within the 23 largest cities and 148 smaller cities. It is clear that that is where the political power is also harboured. As a result it is, by degree, more difficult to get the proper focus of attention that we need for the aspirations of rural Canada. The 9,500 towns and villages, along with the primary producers in agriculture, fishing, mining and forestry, have to knock harder and longer to get attention at the door of society's decision-makers. Simply put, while the hinterlands provide the lion's share of the nation's wealth, the cities harvest the benefit.
Today there are more Members of Parliament representing the urban settlements in and around the Cities of Montreal and Toronto than representing the three prairie provinces and the two northern territories. The three largest cities in Canada, Montreal, Toronto and Vancouver, collectively have more voting power in Parliament than has 85 per cent of Canada's land area. The voting power is such that it is its own concern.
There is a need for Canadian society to refocus on the potential of our hinterland and to diversify our population settlement patterns. It is my view that there is a bias which arises in urban citizens against the country cousins, albeit unintended and certainly without malice. Nevertheless, there is therein a real damage.
I want to set forward a few examples. The first one is relatively harmless and perhaps borders on trivia. I am going to talk about the urban weather reporter. After six weeks of drought in the rural communities, this pesky little fellow, armed with pointer and weather map, appears on our television screens and announces that there is good news, that it will be hot and dry for the weekend. This kind of announcement is
received in rural communities as an insult. It irritates rural people who are dependent upon the weather in a way in which urban communities can hardly imagine.
Who among us can justly claim that Canada Post is acting with justice and fair-mindedness when it provides free door-to-door postal service in urban areas but forces rural people to rent metal mail boxes? Most rural people would never expect door-to-door delivery, but they remain perplexed by the fact that they are charged while urban citizens have a free ride on the public purse.
There is the question of what makes the Post Office remain and what makes it disappear. Canada Post is presently shooting off small rural post offices like clay pigeons. It matters not that rural citizens may have to travel 100 or more miles on a return trip to obtain their mail. It matters not how busy a farmer or rancher is in the sprawling country of southern Alberta. The only consideration of Canada Post is the number of people per mile and whether or not the local post office makes money.
It does not matter that the petroleum and agricultural resources near Big Stone, Alberta, earns Governments $60 million annually. If the local post office loses $5,000 per year, Canada Post will close it down. Moreover, it does not bat an eyelash at free door-to-door delivery in urban communities. The fact that it costs millions of dollars annually to provide the door-to-door service in urban areas is unpersuasive. It is those far away post offices in rural Canada upon which Canada Post pins its hopes for a balanced budget. That is a pattern that may work but it is a pattern which is flooded with shame and insensitivity.
I would like to give the telephone company as another example. This corporate giant is under the jurisdiction of provincial Governments, yet the same sociological forces are exerted. If you are in urban Canada, you can have a private telephone in your home for $8, $9 or $10 a month. For the same price in many parts of rural Canada you can deal on a $130,000 harvest combine while three of your neighbours listen in. We are in the computer age and farmers need private phone lines to access data banks for their computers on accounting, market information, nutritional requirements and veterinary services.
I would now like to talk about the bias that exists in police service. I had occasion to phone the Royal Canadian Mounted Police at Camrose, Alberta, on a Saturday this summer. My call was intercepted and transferred to Red Deer. When I told that to a colleague of mine in the House of Commons, he gave me a better example than my own. At 4 a.m. a man was caught beating his wife. A phone call was made to the police for help. The operator transferred the call to Kamloops, British Columbia, more than 100 miles away from the incident. The officer who received the phone call said that someone from the local detachment would attend at nine o'clock in the morning, some five hours later.
October 8, 1986

I do not raise this point to bring issue with whether the R.C.M.P. should have different working hours or whether they should have time off on the weekends. I think their present hours are fine and we all recognize they should have time off on the weekends. However, I do emphasize that rural people accept a level of police protection which urban people would never tolerate. If police protection is not continuous, it is not secure.
1 want to talk a bit about labour disputes, which are usually an urban phenomenon, and their impact on rural Canada. Most people, from following recent strikes in Thunder Bay and Vancouver, know that the labour workers are seeking more money. Many people would not even argue about whether they ought to receive more, but many of them do not recognize that when the workers and grain handlers get more money, the farmers get less. The situation is literally that the farmers receive international price, less cost. In other words, the administration, handling, shipping and transportation costs are all deducted.
We have a situation in our agricultural communities in Canada today where our farmers have had a decreased income every year for five years and this year have had a 20 per cent decrease over the previous year. It is within that scenario that the urban worker rises up to say that he wants more even though it means that the agricultural producers who provided the jobs in the first place must accept less so the labourers can have more. It is another example which underscores the fact that there is a sociological phenomenon that favours urban Canadians over rural Canadians.
I am proud that my Government announced in the Speech from the Throne that there will be more focus on day care. Urban Canada is crying out for more day care, more space and services and the commitment of more money. There is no day care in rural Canada in spite of the fact that in my Province of Alberta, 41 per cent of farmers or farmers and their spouses work off the farm. The farm environment is more dangerous for young children, with chemicals, machinery and animals. Yet world conditions and economic pressures on farmers mean that some 53 per cent of farmers, on a national average, now have off-farm work. However, there is still no day care. I am pleased with the initiative and I hope that those who design the actual legislation and initiative will remember that rural Canada also needs day care along with our urban cousin.
Let me give one final example-the pricing of farm chemicals-and I will move on to solutions that I believe will be helpful. Banvel and Dycleer are two chemicals. Banvel is used by farmers and Dycleer is used by municipal Governments. Dycleer is exactly the same chemical as Banvel, yet it sells for $20 a unit cheaper. It is illegal to use it for agricultural purposes. The company argues that this is because of its packaging and selling. Yet there are people in the farm aerial spray business who buy even more of the chemical than the municipalities, yet have to pay more for no other reason than
The Address-Mr. Malone
that they are classified as agricultural operations. That type of focus should not continue.
Let me ask rhetorically: Is Canada better off if Toronto and Montreal become as large as New York? Are we better off if Vancouver and Halifax become the Chicagos and Detroits of Canada? Are there no limits to growth? Is not the hinterland something we should focus on for increased vitality?
I believe, because of my past experience in the Province of Alberta, that it is possible to refocus on our hinterland and create a new vitality in it.
In the mid-1970s the Alberta Government decentralized and gave a sense of fresh air to many of those communities that were struggling. For instance, when Water Resources was moved to the community of Vegreville and the Alberta Development Corporation moved its headquarters from Edmonton to Camrose, it brought a new breath of fresh air and vitality to those communities. The community of Rimbey is a town of 600 in the riding of the Hon. Member for Wetas-kiwin (Mr. Schellenberger). It now has the provincial offices of the provincial parks programs and it is much more able to sustain itself. Yet there are parts of east central Alberta and west central Saskatchewan that are dying and crying out for the attention that goes to urban Canada, to start moving toward a rural focus, closer to the people who are served.
I could go on much longer and give many examples to show the kind of discrimination that takes place, but I want to talk about some solutions that we might offer.
First, I believe we should have a decentralized Government wherever possible. The Farm Credit Corporation, for example, could move to Honna, Alberta, an area that is losing its population because it depended on being a railway centre. Now that that industry is fading away, it needs some injection of a resource that will give it a new sense of vitality.
1 ask, partly tongue in check, if there would be anything wrong with moving the national headquarters of Canada Post to Come-By-Chance, Newfoundland? It seems to me that that is a very logical place to put the headquarters of Canada Post. It might be appropriate in terms of rural reconstruction and having the citizens of Canada recognize that we finally put the Post Office in its right location.
Perhaps the Animal Health Division of the Department of Agriculture could go to Innisfail, Alberta. Could the plant science branch not go to a rural community in Saskatchewan? Why must all these operations be harboured in Ottawa? If we were to move some of the operations of the federal Government from Ottawa, into the hinterland that is so important and needed for the continued growth of our country, we could have greater and more vital communities. We should do more with the industrial infrastructure and, wherever possible, use incentives to move it so that the major developments do not always take place in Montreal, Toronto, London, Hamilton or Vancouver but in little communities like-

speechtext:
-Craigmyle, Alberta, a perfect example. I know the Hon. Minister of Fisheries and Oceans (Mr. Siddon) recognizes that he is speaking about a region of Canada that has a decreasing population.
It is important that I point out that according to the old Canada Works Program, communities with low unemployment rates would only get $100,000 for the area. The logic used by Statistics Canada was that areas with a low unemployment rate did not need any more money to improve the unemployment situation in the area. However, this logic did not take into account that many of those rural communities exported their unemployed, as boys and girls growing up on the farm in the Prairies did not stay unless they could take over the farm. They would go to the city where they would be listed on the city's unemployment roll, when unemployed.
A few years ago I attended the opening of a factory at Bashaw. I had the pleasure of seeing 30 young people, dressed in white cloaks and caps, working in that new cheese factory. I asked each of them where they were from and what they would be doing if they were not working in that factory. Each person told me that they would be in Red Deer, Calgary or Edmonton. Young people give us low unemployment statistics because they move away, but if industry is brought into those rural communities they will stay home. We must change the trend.
Finally, while it would be easy to blame previous Governments for this diminishing population in rural Canada, I do not want to do that because I believe that this trend existed for logical reasons. 1 believe there were natural efficiencies that made us move to urban areas to fulfil our goals, but today is different and we live in an age of the computer and high tech communication. It is interesting to note, for instance, that on Galiano Island and other islands off the coast of British Columbia there are major executives of large corporations' who basically run those corporations from their homes. Because of technology today we have the capacity to revitalize. It is a new phenomenon that we can do what we could not have done 10 years ago.
I see my time is up. I have other solutions to which I wanted to refer, but perhaps someone will ask me about an elected Senate and on that note, I will sit down.
